name: British Vernacular

description.short: The unselfconscious regional building of the English countryside — Cotswold limestone, thatch, cob, and brick — later mined by revivalists for a whole century of cottage imagery.
description.long:
Regional vernacular in Britain is defined by geology. The Cotswolds build in oolitic limestone with stone-slate roofs because that is what the ground yields; East Anglia builds in flint and timber; the West Country in cob. Each produces a distinct language of wall thickness, roof pitch, opening size, and colour without any of it being designed.

The revival of this material from the 1890s onward — and its export to America as the Cotswold cottage and the Storybook style — is a case worth studying closely: a building culture generated entirely by local constraint, reproduced in places where none of those constraints apply.

defining_characteristics: Material determined by local geology, and everything else following from it
Steep roofs sized to the covering material — thatch, stone slate, or clay tile
Small irregular openings and very thick walls
Growth by accretion, producing irregular plans and rooflines
No designer, no date, no name
